idiom_name: scala.util.Using: Using.resource / Using.apply / Using.Manager over AutoCloseable or a Using.Releasable instance
implementation_notes: The JVM has no deterministic destruction and Scala adds none, so the standard library (2.13+) supplies scala.util.Using: Using.resource(r) { body } releases on every path and lets the body's exception propagate, Using(r) { body } wraps use and release in a Try (a release failure becomes a suppressed exception on a failing body), and Using.Manager registers arbitrarily many resources inside one bracket with LIFO release; a Using.Releasable instance teaches it to release types that do not implement AutoCloseable. The classic owner object is replaced by an AutoCloseable plus these combinators; the pre-2.13 Loan Pattern - a method that takes a by-name body and releases in finally - is the same idea hand-written, and Using exists because that hand-written form repeats the release and loses teardown errors.
pitfalls: Using releases only what is passed as the resource (or registered with the Manager) inside the bracket: opening a second resource in the body without registering it recreates the leak, and returning a resource out of the bracket returns it after release.

Release failures do not fail a failing operation: with the exception-carrying forms a release error is only a suppressed exception, and with Using.apply it surfaces only when the body succeeded - flush/commit explicitly when the data matters.

Relying on JVM finalizers or Cleaner for pooled, locked or leased resources is not RAII: release is delayed to GC/phantom reachability and may never happen before shutdown, which shows up as pool exhaustion rather than as a crash.
